## The Problem

```r
calculate_mean <- function(x) {


  mean(x)

}

calculate_mean("hello")
#> Warning: argument is not numeric or logical
#> [1] NA
```

::: {.notes}
R has no static type checking.

You write a function expecting numbers. Someone passes text. You only find out at runtime - or worse, in production.

In large codebases, these bugs are hard to trace. The error message points to mean(), not to the real problem: the wrong argument was passed.
:::

---

## The Solution: rdoc {auto-animate=true}

```r
#' Calculate the mean
#'
#' @param x A numeric vector
#' @return The mean value
calculate_mean <- function(x) mean(x)
```

::: {.notes}
Here's standard roxygen2 documentation. The param and return tags describe arguments and return values, but types are implicit.
:::

## The Solution: rdoc {auto-animate=true}

```r
#' Calculate the mean
#'
#' @typedParam x {class_numeric} A numeric vector
#' @typedReturn {class_numeric} The mean value
calculate_mean <- function(x) mean(x)
```

Minimal changes to your roxygen2 syntax.

::: {.notes}
With rdoc, just change param to typedParam, return to typedReturn, and add the type in braces.

The key difference: these annotations are enforced by the linter.
:::

---

## Catch Errors Before Runtime

```r
calculate_mean("hello")
#
# Linter warning:
# Argument 'x' expects class_numeric, got class_character
```

::: {.notes}
When someone calls your function with the wrong type, the linter catches it immediately - before the code ever runs.

This integrates with lintr and the R language server. You see the error right in your editor, as you type.
:::

---

## Expressive Type Syntax

```r
#' @typedParam x {NULL | class_numeric}
#'   Optional numeric vector
#'
#' @typedParam callback {class_function}
#'   Function to apply
#'
#' @typedParam ... {class_any}
#'   Additional arguments
```

::: {.notes}
The type syntax is expressive. You can declare nullable types, union types, and typed ellipsis.

This covers the patterns R developers actually use.
:::

---

## Built on S7

```r
# Define your own S7 class
person <- S7::new_class("person",
  properties = list(
    name = S7::class_character,
    age = S7::class_integer
  )
)

#' @typedParam x {person} A person object
greet <- function(x) {

  paste0("Hello, ", x@name)
}
```

::: {.notes}
Under the hood, rdoc is built on S7.

S7 class objects are the source of truth - not string matching. This means the type system understands class hierarchies. And your custom S7 classes are supported out of the box.

rdoc builds on roxygen2, lintr, and S7 - tools the R community already uses.
:::

---

## Getting Started

```yaml
# .lintr
linters: lintr::linters_with_defaults(
    type_consistency = rdoc::type_consistency_linter()
  )
```

Packages can also export type metadata for their functions.

::: {.notes}
Getting started is simple. Add rdoc's linter to your .lintr configuration file.

Once configured, type checking works automatically with lintr and the R language server.

Package authors can also export type metadata, so users get type checking when calling your package functions.
:::

---

## rdoc

Static type checking for R.

Catch type errors before runtime.

Works with scripts, packages, and box modules.

github.com/calderonsamuel/rdoc

::: {.notes}
rdoc brings static type checking to R.

It works with standalone scripts, R packages, and box modules. It integrates with the tools you already use. And it catches type errors before they become runtime surprises.
